query: Prior to high-frequency execution, were stat-arb managers more likely to target mean-reversion of individual spread half-lives rather than emphasize portfolio-level Sharpe optimization?
response:
Yes, prior to the rise of high-frequency trading, statistical arbitrage (stat-arb) managers often focused on mean-reversion strategies targeting individual spread half-lives. This approach involved identifying pairs or groups of securities that historically reverted to a mean price relationship. The emphasis was typically on exploiting short-term price discrepancies based on historical correlations.

In contrast, portfolio-level Sharpe optimization became more prominent with the advent of high-frequency trading, as it allowed for more sophisticated risk management and the ability to optimize returns across a broader set of trades in real-time. High-frequency strategies often leverage technology to execute trades at speeds that make portfolio-level optimization more feasible and effective.
